title: My Own Secret Strategy For The First Day Of School
author: Michael Linsin
summary: This piece lays out Michael Linsin's personal, previously unpublished first-day-of-school tactic: casually announce one specific rule and its consequence early in the greeting, then calmly enforce it the moment a student tests it. The goal isn't the rule itself but the demonstration — showing new students, within the first few minutes, that the teacher does exactly what they say they'll do. Linsin recommends silence during instructions for elementary and middle schoolers, and a no-phones rule for high schoolers, precisely because those are the rules most likely to be broken quickly. The follow-through must be unhurried, calm, and free of visible anger so it reads as confident modeling rather than punishment. Done right, he argues, this single quiet act can compress weeks of the normal 'testing phase' into a single moment, because it proves the teacher's word is trustworthy before any full classroom management plan has even been taught.
points: Announce one specific rule and its consequence casually within the first few minutes of greeting new students, before covering anything else.
Choose a rule likely to be broken quickly — staying silent during instructions for younger students, hidden phones for high schoolers.
When the rule is broken, enforce the stated consequence calmly and unhurriedly, without anger, as a deliberate demonstration of follow-through.
This early enforcement models how all future misbehavior will be handled and signals that the teacher can be trusted to do what they say.
The strategy is only a temporary bridge into teaching the full classroom management plan, not a replacement for it.
quotes: The strategy, which takes just a few seconds, sends a powerful message to your new students. It gets to the quick, ending any doubt about whether you’re a teacher who will do what you say you will.
It’s a bit sneaky and may need adjusting according to your grade level, but it effectively eliminates the testing phase whereby students push and probe to find the limits of your patience.
For elementary students I recommend asking them to stay silent while you’re talking. This can also work for middle school.
So for high-schoolers I recommend asking them to keep their phones out of sight and letting them know that you’ll take them away if you see them.
Now, it’s important that you do this after a long pause, and be sure to take your time. You want every student to see you doing what you said without showing any anger or frustration.
Furthermore, because no other teacher does this—after all, who in their right mind would hold someone accountable in the first few minutes—it says volumes about you and what you value.
Smile, do what you say, and they’ll respect and appreciate you right from the get-go.
